```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

# Simulate coral bleaching
N <- 24
peak_sst <- rnorm(N, mean = 30, sd = 1.5)
beta_0 <- -90
beta_1 <- 3
logit_pbleach <- beta_0 + beta_1 * peak_sst
pbleach <- plogis(logit_pbleach)
bleach <- rbinom(N, 1, pbleach)
reefs <- tibble(peak_sst, bleach)

bleach_lm <- lm(bleach ~ peak_sst, reefs)
bleach_lm_pred <- tibble(
  peak_sst = seq(min(reefs$peak_sst), max(reefs$peak_sst), length.out = 100)
)
bleach_lm_pred$bleach <- predict(bleach_lm, newdata = bleach_lm_pred)
bleach_lm_b0 <- signif(coef(bleach_lm)[["(Intercept)"]], 2)
bleach_lm_b1 <- signif(coef(bleach_lm)[["peak_sst"]], 2)

# Little brown bat detections
bats <- read_csv("data/5bat_count_data-21682.csv") |>
  filter(Species == "Myotis lucifugus")
bat_summary <- bats |>
  summarize(p_detected = mean(detected), .by = Year)

bat_glm <- glm(detected ~ Year, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = bats)
bat_glm_pred <- tibble(
  Year = seq(min(bats$Year), max(bats$Year), length.out = 100)
)
bat_glm_pred$logitp_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  newdata = bat_glm_pred,
  type = "link"
)
bat_glm_pred$p_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  newdata = bat_glm_pred,
  type = "response"
)

bat_glm_points <- tibble(
  Year = c(
    min(bats$Year),
    -coef(bat_glm)[["(Intercept)"]] / coef(bat_glm)[["Year"]],
    max(bats$Year)
  )
)
bat_glm_points$logitp_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  newdata = bat_glm_points,
  type = "link"
)
bat_glm_points$p_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  newdata = bat_glm_points,
  type = "response"
)

bat_b0 <- signif(coef(bat_glm)[["(Intercept)"]], 4)
bat_b1 <- signif(coef(bat_glm)[["Year"]], 4)
bat_term <- \(year) signif(abs(bat_b1) * year, 4)
bat_logit <- \(year) signif(bat_b0 - bat_term(year), 4)
bat_p <- \(year) signif(plogis(bat_logit(year)), 2)
```

# Logistic regression

## Learning objectives

- **Explain** why a linear model doesn't work for a binary outcome
- **Convert** probabilities to log odds
- **Interpret** the coefficients of a logistic regression

# Binary outcomes

## Does heat stress make corals bleach?

Peak sea surface temperature and bleaching at `r N` reefs (simulated data).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(reefs, aes(peak_sst, bleach)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (°C)", y = "Bleached")
```

## Fit a linear model

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(reefs, aes(peak_sst, bleach)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = bleach_lm_pred, color = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (°C)", y = "Bleached")
```

## The problems

::: {.incremental}

1. Bleaching is binary (0 or 1), but the predictions are continuous
   - Solution: treat the prediction as the _probability_ of bleaching
2. The predictions can be less than 0 or more than 1
   - "When peak SST is 32°C, the probability of bleaching is `r round(predict(bleach_lm, tibble(peak_sst = 32)), 1)`." That doesn't make any sense!

:::

::: {.fragment}

How do we keep our predictions between 0 and 1?

:::

# Introducing the log odds

## Different ranges

Our linear model, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, can take on _any value_. Its range is $(-\infty, \infty)$.

Probabilities are limited. Their range is $[0, 1]$.

We need a function that converts values from $[0, 1]$ to $(-\infty, \infty)$.

## From probabilities to odds

The _odds_ are the ratio $\frac{p}{1 - p}$: the probability of success relative to failure.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

ggplot() +
  stat_function(fun = \(x) x / (1 - x), n = 1e4) +
  xlim(0, 0.999) +
  labs(x = "Probability", y = "Odds")
```

Probabilities live in $[0, 1]$. Odds live in $[0, \infty)$. We're halfway there!

## From odds to log odds

The _log odds_ convert probabilities from $[0, 1]$ to $(-\infty, \infty)$. We call this function the _logit_:

$$
\text{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)
$$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

ggplot() +
  stat_function(fun = \(x) log(x / (1 - x)), n = 1e4) +
  xlim(0.001, 0.999) +
  labs(x = "Probability", y = "Log odds")
```

# Regressing probabilities

## Without the log odds

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Bleaching} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
p &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PeakSST}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\beta_0 = `r bleach_lm_b0`, \beta_1 = `r bleach_lm_b1`$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(reefs, aes(peak_sst, bleach)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = bleach_lm_pred, color = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (°C)", y = "Bleached")
```

## What the model means

$\text{Bleaching}$ is a $\text{Bernoulli}$ random variable. It "succeeds" with probability $p$. E.g., for a sample of 10 reefs with $p = 0.3$, we would expect $10 \times 0.3 = 3$ reefs to bleach.

The probability of bleaching, $p$, changes with $\text{PeakSST}$.

```{r}
tibble(peak_sst = c(27, 29, 31, 33)) |>
  mutate(p = predict(bleach_lm, newdata = pick(everything()))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Peak SST (°C)", "$p$"), digits = 2)
```

::: {.fragment}

Uh oh! Probabilities outside $[0, 1]$ are meaningless.

:::

## Use the log odds, AKA the _logit_

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Bleaching} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PeakSST}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\beta_0 = `r beta_0`, \beta_1 = `r beta_1`$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(reefs, aes(peak_sst, bleach)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3) +
  geom_function(
    fun = \(x) plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x),
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (°C)", y = "Bleached")
```

## A nifty little trick

Check that out! Instead of saying $p$ changes linearly with $\text{PeakSST}$, we say $\text{logit}(p)$ does.

The predictions now stay between 0 and 1.

## Logistic vs linear regression

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Linear:** a line, with normally distributed residuals around it

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

**Logistic:** a binary outcome. The "line" is now a probability and it's curved.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

:::

# An example

## Little brown bats and white-nose syndrome


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

![NPS Photo / von Linden](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/images/wns-vonLinden.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false&quality=78&format=webp)

:::

::: {.column style="font-size: 0.8em"}

Johnson et al. (2021) surveyed `r n_distinct(bats$Site)` sites in the Monongahela National Forest (`r min(bats$Year)` - `r max(bats$Year)`) for little brown bats. 

White-nose syndrome has been documented in West Virginia since 2009.

If the infection is harming little brown bat populations, the probability of detecting a bat should decline.

:::

:::

## The data

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_summary,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("Detected", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))
```

## The model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Detected} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Year}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Fit the model

```{r}
#| class-output: small-output

summary(bat_glm)
```

## Interpreting the coefficients

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Detected} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \text{Year}
\end{aligned}
$$

The _log odds_ decrease by `r abs(bat_b1)` year^-1^.

Not terribly intuitive. Let's convert to probabilities.

## From log odds to probabilities {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

In 2003:

| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \text{Year}$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \times 2003$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r bat_term(2003)`$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_logit(2003)`$]{.fragment}
| [$\hphantom{\text{logit}()}p = `r bat_p(2003)`$]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment}

There was an `r bat_p(2003) * 100`% chance of detecting a little brown bat at a site in 2003.

:::

:::

::: {.column}

In 2019:

| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \text{Year}$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \times 2019$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r bat_term(2019)`$]{.fragment}
| [$\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_logit(2019)`$]{.fragment}
| [$\hphantom{\text{logit}()}p = `r bat_p(2019)`$]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment}

There was a `r bat_p(2019) * 100`% chance of detecting a little brown bat at a site in 2019.

:::

:::

:::

::: {.fragment}

That tiny coefficient (`r abs(bat_b1)`) represents a _huge_ decline over the study period!

:::

## Visualize the prediction

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Detected} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \text{Year}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(bat_glm_pred, aes(x = Year, y = logitp_detected)) +
  geom_line(color = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(
    data = bat_glm_points,
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    size = 4,
    stroke = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_label(
    aes(label = c(bat_logit(2003), 0, bat_logit(2019))),
    data = bat_glm_points,
    hjust = c(0, 0, 1),
    vjust = c(0, 0, 1),
    nudge_x = c(0.5, 0.5, -0.5),
    size = 6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  labs(y = "logit(p)")
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_glm_pred,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_glm_points,
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    size = 4,
    stroke = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_label(
    aes(y = p_detected, label = c(bat_p(2003), 0.5, bat_p(2019))),
    data = bat_glm_points,
    hjust = c(0, 0, 1),
    vjust = c(0, 0, 1),
    nudge_x = c(0.5, 0.5, -0.5),
    size = 6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("Detected", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))
```

:::

:::

# Recap

## Logistic regression, visualized

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Detected} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Year}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_glm_pred,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("Detected", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))
```

:::

:::

## Key points

::: {.fragment}

**How do we model binary responses?**

As a Bernoulli variable, where $p$ varies with the predictor.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Why do we need the logit?**

It links the linear equation (any value) to valid probabilities (0 to 1).

:::

::: {.fragment}

**How do we interpret logistic regression coefficients?**

They're not intuitive, so visualize the model predictions.

:::

Johnson, C., Brown, D. J., Sanders, C., & Stihler, C. W. (2021).
